pages.title: India-Pakistan: Cohen's paired minority conflict
pages.summary: A diagram shows Pakistan placed between India and China (linked by CPEC), with the USA, Russia, China, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Turkey as friends because of its location next to Central Asia. Cites Stephen P. Cohen's Shooting for a Century, which calls the conflict a paired minority conflict and a mutually hurting stalemate that may last another 30 years.

pages.title: Nehru's view and Pakistan as pivot state
pages.summary: Says India's Pakistan policy is criticised as a posture rather than a policy, and that Nehru wrongly expected Pakistan to return to India. Cites Lieven on Pakistan's strong foundation, and Ian Bremmer and Andrew Korybko calling it a pivot or zipper state because of its location.

pages.title: Pakistan's army, deep state and Kashmir identity
pages.summary: Argues Pakistan is not isolated, that its Army, the deep state, draws legitimacy by projecting India as a threat, and that talking to Rawalpindi is unrealistic. Says Kashmir is a clash of two identities, so even resolving it would not improve relations.

pages.title: Indira and Rajiv Gandhi's Pakistan policies
pages.summary: Describes Indira Gandhi's realist approach, called India's Monroe Doctrine, and the intervention that created Bangladesh as a military victory but diplomatic failure. Under Rajiv Gandhi, Kashmir terrorism gained a transnational dimension as the US promoted Mujahiddin in Afghanistan.

pages.title: Gujral Doctrine and Vajpayee's nuclear decision
pages.summary: The Gujral Doctrine sought a peaceful periphery through Panchsheel plus two principles and brought the Mahakali Treaty, the Ganga water agreement and visa liberalisation. Vajpayee said neighbours cannot be changed, but his decision to go nuclear legitimised Pakistan's weapon and began an arms race.

pages.title: Nuclear fallout, Kargil, ceasefire and Lahore
pages.summary: Pakistan gained strategic balance, leaving India vulnerable to proxy wars and nuclear blackmail, and its unofficial doctrine does not adhere to no first use. Kargil, nuclear CBMs, the 2003 LoC ceasefire and bus diplomacy leading to the Lahore Declaration follow.

pages.title: Manmohan Doctrine and Modi's neighbourhood policy
pages.summary: Manmohan Singh's economic diplomacy stressed trade, people contact and an informal Musharraf formula on Kashmir, but relations worsened from 2011. Modi began with neighbourhood first and invited SAARC leaders, which the notes say will not work for Pakistan.

pages.title: Modi's present approach and three cards
pages.summary: Lists the present approach: isolating Pakistan, making terrorism the main issue and considering military options such as revising no first use. According to C Raja Mohan, Modi uses Baluchistan, Gilgit Baltistan and the Indus water treaty, and the page begins describing Baluchistan's forced integration and Punjabi dominance.

pages.title: Baluchistan card and its importance for India
pages.summary: Describes Baloch exploitation, the 2006 killing of Akbar Bugti, army abuses and Quetta as a Haqqani Network centre. Explains that India raised Baluchistan under Modi, having first accepted it as a talking point at Sharm-al-Sheikh, and links its importance to the CPEC corridor.

pages.title: Gilgit Baltistan issue
pages.summary: Describes Gilgit Baltistan as part of Jammu and Kashmir, leased by the British, with Shia people and an undefined constitutional status in Pakistan. Notes that Pakistan considering a fifth province is opposed by India and Kashmir separatists, who fear it would ease ending Article 370.

pages.title: Indus Water Treaty: allocation and Pakistan's veto
pages.summary: Per Chellaney, Pakistan gets the three western rivers (80% of the water) and India the three eastern rivers, with Pakistan holding a veto over Indian projects. Disputes go to the Indus commission, then neutral experts, then arbitration, and Pakistan's irrigation depends heavily on the water.

pages.title: Using the Indus treaty as a card
pages.summary: Says the Modi government wants to review the treaty and use India's western river rights, as blood and water cannot flow together. Lists reasons against using it as a card (nuclear risk, moral high ground, China and the Brahmaputra, responsible image) and begins the arguments in favour.

pages.title: Experts on Pakistan policy: Chellaney to Narayanan
pages.summary: Finishes the case for using the Indus treaty, including suspending commission meetings, then contrasts Chellaney, Pant and Raja Mohan, who want to raise stakes, with Suhasini Haidar and Pratap Bhanu Mehta, who oppose tit for tat. M K Narayanan urges restraint and cyber warfare instead of the Baluchistan card.

pages.title: Mehta, Raja Mohan and Happymon Jacob
pages.summary: Mehta calls restraint a deterrence, not defeatism, in a game of many moves. Raja Mohan says the government has abandoned the two-track approach and is raising stakes, while Jacob warns that a military option is not worth its cost and quick fixes will fail.

pages.title: Jacob's creative statecraft and Tharoor's Pax India
pages.summary: Jacob calls for creative statecraft, adequate security steps and addressing Kashmiri alienation. Shashi Tharoor's Pax India lists back channel diplomacy, raising the international community's stake in India's economy, using India's weight in financial institutions, a terrorism convention and communal harmony.

pages.title: Siachen: Cohen's comb analogy and the issue
pages.summary: Cohen likens the fight to two bald men fighting for a comb, yet the notes say Siachen matters strategically and as a water source. Explains the LoC undemarcated beyond NJ 9842, the rival alignments, and India's 1984 Operation Meghdoot occupying the Saltoro ridge.

pages.title: Siachen: composite dialogue and rival positions
pages.summary: Siachen was a doable issue in the composite dialogue, with Manmohan Singh wanting a mountain of peace but the Indian Army opposing. India wants demarcation, delineation and authentication before demilitarisation, with penalties, while Pakistan wants demilitarisation first.

pages.title: Sir Creek: dispute, impact and 1914 map
pages.summary: Describes Sir Creek as a 96 km estuary whose unsettled maritime boundary blocks use of ocean wealth and leads to fishermen being caught. Explains the UNCLOS deadline and the contested 1914 map, with paragraph 9 giving the Green line and paragraph 10 the thalweg principle.

pages.title: Sir Creek: 1925 map and thalweg arguments
pages.summary: India backs the 1925 map's mid-channel Red line, while Pakistan rejects the thalweg principle because the creek is marshy land. India says it is navigable at high tides, and the notes call its case stronger since Sind and Kutchcha built pillars along the mid-channel.

flashcards.front: How does Stephen P. Cohen characterise the India-Pakistan conflict in Shooting for a Century?
flashcards.back: As a 'paired minority conflict', compared with Arab-Jews and Shia-Sunni conflicts, and as a mutually hurting stalemate in which India cannot lose and Pakistan cannot win. He expects another 30 years of shooting before normalisation is possible.

flashcards.front: Why would resolving Kashmir not by itself normalise India-Pakistan relations?
flashcards.back: Kashmir is a clash of two exclusive identities: India as a secular state and Pakistan as a separate homeland for the subcontinent's minorities. The Pakistan Army, which gains legitimacy by projecting India as a threat, is the second obstacle.

flashcards.front: How do the notes assess the Bangladesh war under Indira Gandhi?
flashcards.back: As a military victory but a diplomatic failure, since India gained no advantage. It deepened the Pakistan Army's revenge motive, led to low-intensity warfare, and Bangladesh moved to a pro-Pakistan faction after Mujibur Rehman's assassination.

flashcards.front: What were the features and outcomes of the Gujral Doctrine?
flashcards.back: It added two principles to Panchsheel: India acts as an elder brother, not a big brother, and gives concessions provided neighbours do not let their territory be used for terrorism against India. Outcomes included the Mahakali Treaty, the Ganga water agreement and visa liberalisation with Pakistan.

flashcards.front: How did the nuclear decision under Vajpayee leave India more vulnerable?
flashcards.back: It legitimised Pakistan's nuclear weapon and gave Pakistan strategic balance, exposing India to proxy wars and nuclear blackmail. Pakistan's unofficial doctrine does not adhere to no first use, and Pakistan then tested India's claims at Kargil.

flashcards.front: Which three cards has the Modi government used against Pakistan, according to C Raja Mohan?
flashcards.back: Baluchistan, Gilgit Baltistan and the Indus water treaty. The idea is to speak in the language Pakistan understands and to strike where it hurts more.

flashcards.front: How does the Indus Water Treaty divide the rivers, and what veto does Pakistan hold?
flashcards.back: Pakistan gets the western rivers (Jhelum, Chenab, Indus), holding 80% of the water, and India the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej). India can carry out western-river projects only with Pakistan's consent, and disputes go to the Indus commission, neutral experts, then arbitration.

flashcards.front: What is Pratap Bhanu Mehta's argument for strategic restraint towards Pakistan?
flashcards.back: He says it is a game of many moves and Pakistan is not a normal state. Restraint is not defeatism but a deterrence, because it denies Pakistan the opportunity it wants.

flashcards.front: What are India's and Pakistan's negotiating positions on Siachen?
flashcards.back: India favours demilitarisation only after boundaries are demarcated, delineated and authenticated, with a penalty clause for violations. Pakistan wants to demilitarise first, then demarcate and authenticate, as it sees India in a dominating position.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the Green line and the Red line in the Sir Creek dispute?
flashcards.back: The Green line comes from paragraph 9 of the 1914 map, which Pakistan supports, and puts the boundary east of the creek. The Red line follows the 1925 map, dividing the water from the middle by the thalweg principle, which India supports.

answers.question: Trace the evolution of India's Pakistan policy from Indira Gandhi to the present government and assess its consistency.
answers.intro: The notes call Pakistan India's biggest strategic challenge and criticise India's policy as a posture lacking consistency. Each prime minister has sought a legacy, from Indira Gandhi's realism and Gujral's conciliation to Vajpayee's nuclear turn and Modi's isolation of Pakistan.
body: Indira Gandhi's realist approach, called India's Monroe Doctrine, led to intervention that created Bangladesh; the notes judge it a military victory but diplomatic failure that fuelled Pakistan Army revenge and low-intensity warfare.

Rajiv Gandhi continued this line as Kashmir terrorism gained a transnational dimension. Gujral sought a peaceful periphery with conditional concessions, yielding the Mahakali Treaty, the Ganga water agreement and visa liberalisation.

Vajpayee went nuclear, which legitimised Pakistan's weapon, began an arms race and exposed India to proxy wars, nuclear blackmail and Kargil; pressure then produced nuclear CBMs, the 2003 LoC ceasefire and the Lahore Declaration.
Manmohan Singh pursued trade, people contact and an informal Musharraf formula on Kashmir, nearing a resolution of Sir Creek and Siachen, but relations deteriorated from 2011.

Modi began with neighbourhood first, then isolated Pakistan, insisted terror and talk cannot go together, and used the Baluchistan, Gilgit Baltistan and Indus cards, with informal talk of revising no first use.
scholars: Stephen P. Cohen (Shooting for a Century)
answers.conclusion: India's Pakistan policy has swung between conciliation and coercion, each phase constrained by Pakistan's army, nuclear weapons and terrorism. A durable policy needs clear goals, a realistic reading of Pakistan, and consistency rather than postures.

answers.question: India's Pakistan policy oscillates between raising the stakes and strategic restraint. Critically evaluate the options debated by scholars, with reference to the Indus Water Treaty and Baluchistan.
answers.intro: The Modi government has moved from engagement to raising stakes through Baluchistan, Gilgit Baltistan and the Indus treaty. Scholars are divided between hitting where it hurts and a restraint that preserves India's image and options.
body: Case for raising stakes: Chellaney, Harsh Pant and C Raja Mohan favour it, and Raja Mohan notes the government has dropped the two-track approach for military readiness and counter-terrorism, though critics say it offers postures, not action.

Indus card: Pakistan gets 80% of the water and holds a veto. Supporters call it the most effective card and note India can suspend commission meetings; opponents cite nuclear risk, lost moral high ground and China on the Brahmaputra.
Baluchistan card: forcibly integrated and exploited, hosting Taliban safe havens at Quetta and sitting on the CPEC corridor, it is useful leverage, yet Narayanan prefers cyber warfare.
Case for restraint: Narayanan wants a mature image, Mehta calls restraint deterrence, Suhasini Haidar doubts tit for tat, and Happymon Jacob says nuclear risk is irrational.
Tharoor's Pax India suggests back channel diplomacy, a larger international stake in India's economy, weight in financial institutions, a terrorism convention and communal harmony.
answers.conclusion: Neither pure coercion nor passive restraint answers a conflict of identity with a nuclear-armed neighbour. India needs calibrated pressure, security readiness, international leverage and attention to Kashmiri alienation, pursued with consistency and an eye on the grand picture.
